reference.title: hundred, thousand, million
reference.text: Say and after hundred: two hundred and ten. hundred, thousand, and million have no -s after a number: five thousand, six million. In decimals say point, not dot: four point three.

reference.title: Saying approximate numbers
reference.text: about 500 · at least 12 a day · between 2,000 and 3,000

reference.why: No -s on thousand after a number.
British English uses and after hundred.

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). Ask the student these questions one at a time: When’s your birthday? What’s the number of your house or building? What’s the population of your town or city? What’s the average price of buying or renting a two-bedroom flat there? tasks.instruction: How fast is your life? Answer the questionnaire with often, sometimes, or never. Then listen to your result
tasks.note: SB 1a+1b + Communication 5A (p.109): ИИ задаёт 6 вопросов анкеты, считает баллы (never 1, sometimes 2, often 3) и читает результат из книги; ученик говорит, согласен ли

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate) doing the questionnaire ‘How fast is your life?’. Ask the student these questions one at a time and wait for an answer with often, sometimes, or never (ask ‘Why?’ or ‘Can you give an example?’ once or twice): 1 Do people tell you that you talk too quickly? 2 Do you get impatient when other people are talking? 3 Are you the first person to finish at mealtimes? 4 When you are walking along a street, do you feel frustrated when you are behind people who are walking more slowly? 5 Do you get irritable if you sit for an hour without doing anything, e.g. waiting for the doctor? 6 Do you walk out of shops and restaurants if there is a queue? Count the points: never = 1, sometimes = 2, often = 3. Then tell the student the total and read the result. 6–9: ‘You are living life in the slow lane. Compared to most people, you take things easy and don’t get stressed by modern-day living. You are patient, relaxed, and easy-going. Most of the time this is good news, but sometimes it can be a problem. For example, are you sometimes late for appointments?’ 10–14: ‘You have a medium pace of life. You are probably somebody who can change the speed at which you live depending on the situation.’ 15–18: ‘You are living life in the fast lane, rushing around and trying to do many different activities and projects at the same time. You are impatient and you find it difficult to relax. You are probably very productive, but your relationships and health could suffer as a result.’ Then ask: Do you agree?
exercises.goal: How fast is your life? Answer the questionnaire.
exercises.opener: Let’s do the questionnaire ‘How fast is your life?’. Question 1: do people tell you that you talk too quickly?
criteria: answers all six questions with often, sometimes, or never
adds a reason or an example to at least two answers
says if they agree with the result and why
uses a comparative at least once (e.g. I walk faster than my friends)

steps.text: Answer questions 1–3 with often, sometimes, or never
steps.example: Sometimes. My friends say I talk more quickly when I’m nervous.
Often. I hate walking behind people who are walking more slowly than me.

steps.text: Listen to your result and say if you agree
steps.example: Yes, I agree. I’m quite impatient, especially in the morning.

tasks.context:
I WANT IT, AND I WANT IT NOW! Why are we so impatient?
Tuesday 22 Oct 6:00 am

Whatever happened to patience? We don’t like waiting for things anymore. With faster broadband, instant searches, and immediate downloads, we expect things to happen immediately, and if they don’t we get impatient.

Fast food restaurants have changed the way we eat. The growth of mobile phone apps like Tinder has changed the way we meet new people. We don’t need to wait a week to see the next episode of a TV series – we can download it on Netflix. We are even walking 10% faster than 20 years ago, and talking more quickly. Everything is getting faster, but is it getting better? That depends on how fast you like to live.

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You both read an article about how impatient people are today (50% of users leave a web page that doesn’t load in ten seconds; a third of British people expect a like on Facebook in less than a minute; people wait only 4 minutes for a drink in a bar and 6 minutes for a bus; the most hated time-wasting activities: waiting to be connected on the phone, waiting for a replacement credit card, waiting for a shopping delivery, waiting for a delayed flight, being stuck in traffic). Ask the student the three questions one at a time and give your own short opinion after each answer: 1 Do you think the statistics are true in your country? 2 Which of the ‘time-wasting’ activities annoys you the most? Why? 3 Do you think it’s a good thing that life is getting faster? Why (not)?
exercises.opener: Interesting article! Do you think the statistics are true in your country?
criteria: answers all three questions with reasons (because…)
names one of the time-wasting activities and explains why it annoys them
uses at least one comparative or as…as (e.g. People here are more patient than in Britain)

steps.text: Say if the statistics are true in your country
steps.example: I think they’re true. People here are even more impatient than in Britain.

steps.text: Say which time-wasting activity annoys you most
steps.example: Being stuck in traffic, because I can’t do anything and I’m always late.

steps.text: Say if faster life is a good thing
steps.example: Not really. We do everything more quickly, but we’re more stressed.

tasks.instruction: How has your life changed over the last three years? Answer the questions
tasks.note: SB 4a (вопросы 1–3 анкеты) + 4c → Talk: ИИ спрашивает, ученик отвечает с comparatives

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). Ask the student about how their life has changed over the last three years, one question at a time: 1 Do you spend more or less time… working or studying / getting to work, university, or school / sitting in traffic / talking on the phone / seeing friends / online / sleeping / cooking / shopping / using your computer? Why? (choose four or five of these, one at a time) 2 Do you have more or less free time? Why? 3 What don’t you have time for nowadays? What would you like to have more time for? React to each answer and say something about your own life (e.g. I spend more time studying than before because I’m in my last year at university.). At the end, say whose life has changed more, yours or theirs.
exercises.goal: How has your life changed over the last three years?
exercises.opener: Let’s compare our lives now and three years ago. Do you spend more or less time working or studying? Why?
criteria: uses more / less time + -ing or + noun correctly (I spend more time cooking)
gives a reason with because for most answers
uses comparatives or as…as correctly at least three times
says what they don’t have time for and what they’d like more time for

steps.text: Say if you spend more or less time on different things and why
steps.example: I spend less time sitting in traffic than before because I work from home now.

steps.text: Say if you have more or less free time
steps.example: I have less free time than I did three years ago because I’ve got a baby.

steps.text: Say what you don’t have time for and what you’d like more time for
steps.example: I don’t have time for reading. I’d like to have more time for sport.
